name: Pre-Ride Anxiety Release
description: Calm your nerves before getting in the saddle
instructions: Start with the Karate Chop point on the side of your hand. Tap gently while saying: "Even though I feel nervous about this ride, I deeply and completely accept myself." Continue tapping through the sequence: Eyebrow, Side of Eye, Under Eye, Under Nose, Under Mouth, Collarbone, Under Arm, Top of Head. At each point, acknowledge your feelings: "This nervousness... This anxiety... I choose to feel calm and confident... I am safe... My horse and I are a team." Complete 2-3 rounds until you feel more centered.

name: Connection with Horse
description: Enhance your energetic bond with your horse through tapping
instructions: Do this near your horse if possible. Karate Chop: "Even though we are separate beings, we connect as one." Tap gently: Eyebrow - "I feel my horse's energy..." Side of Eye - "Our hearts align..." Under Eye - "We breathe together..." Under Nose - "Trust flows between us..." Under Mouth - "We understand each other..." Collarbone - "We move as partners..." Under Arm - "Our connection deepens..." Top of Head - "We are one team." Notice how your horse responds to your calm energy.

name: 4-2-6 Performance Breath
description: Performance-based breath pattern to reduce nervous-system activation before transitions or technical work.
instructions:
Inhale for 4 counts.
Hold for 2 counts.
Exhale for 6 counts and repeat.
evidence_base: Sports psychology breath-hold research; HRV optimization.

name: Heart-Focused Breathing
description: Breathing as if in and out of the heart area to increase emotional coherence.
instructions:
Shift attention to the center of your chest.
Breathe slowly as if the breath is moving through your heart space.
Stay with steady rhythm for 10–12 breaths.
evidence_base: HeartMath emotional regulation and coherence training.

name: Five-Sense Horseback Scan
description: On-horse mindfulness exercise using all five senses to anchor rider and horse into the present moment.
instructions:
Place your horse at a relaxed walk or quiet halt in a familiar, safe space.
Scan through sight, sound, touch, smell, and taste, noticing each sensation without judging.
Remain present for 5–10 breaths and observe your horse's feedback.
evidence_base: Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (MBSR), sensory grounding research, equine-assisted mindfulness practices.

name: Mindful Rein Contact Check
description: Mindfulness practice to develop awareness of rein feel, hand tension, and communication with the horse's mouth.
instructions:
Pick up a neutral rein contact.
Notice tension in fingers, wrists, and forearms.
Soften your hands by 5% and observe changes in your horse.
evidence_base: Mindful touch research, equitation science, sports attentional control.

name: Mindful Listening to Arena Sounds
description: Uses mindful hearing to broaden awareness and reduce tunnel vision during riding.
instructions:
At the walk, tune into ambient sounds in and outside the arena.
Label sounds neutrally as 'near', 'far', 'soft', or 'sharp'.
Allow listening to expand your awareness instead of narrowing it.
evidence_base: Mindfulness-based sound grounding, attentional widening research.

name: Visual Horizon Soft-Gaze Practice
description: A visual mindfulness exercise that softens the eyes and expands rider situational awareness.
instructions:
Lift your gaze to the horizon without fixing on a single point.
Soften your peripheral vision and let your eyes relax.
Ride while maintaining wide, calm visual awareness.
evidence_base: Sports psychology visual field expansion, polyvagal theory.

name: Horseback Body Scan
description: A mounted somatic body scan that releases tension and increases awareness of how the rider's body moves with the horse.
instructions:
Place your horse in a relaxed walk or halt.
Slowly scan your body from head to toe, noticing where you are holding tension.
Release tension in small increments and observe how your horse responds.
evidence_base: Somatic experiencing, MBSR body scan, equine-assisted regulation.

name: Conscious Swallow Reset
description: Uses a slow, deliberate swallow to activate vagal pathways and reduce sympathetic arousal.
instructions:
Relax your tongue and jaw and take a slow breath in.
Gently swallow once, noticing the softening in your throat and chest.
Repeat 2–3 times while maintaining steady contact with your horse.
evidence_base: Polyvagal theory and vagal swallowing reflex research.

name: Jaw Release → Horse Release
description: Softening the rider's jaw signals relaxation through the whole body, often resulting in the horse softening as well.
instructions:
Relax your jaw by gently unclenching your teeth and letting your tongue drop from the roof of your mouth.
Take one slow exhale as your jaw softens.
Notice if your horse shows softening signals such as lowering its neck, licking, or blowing out.
evidence_base: Somatic jaw release, equine-rider tension mirroring.

name: Shoulder Rolls (Micro-Movement)
description: Uses small shoulder rolls to release guarding and improve upper-body softness while mounted.
instructions:
Roll your shoulders gently forward and then back in small circles.
Keep the movement tiny so as not to unbalance the horse.
Pair the roll with a slow exhale.
evidence_base: Somatic micro-movement therapy, postural release.

name: TRE-Style Leg Soft Shake
description: A micro-version of tension release (TRE) using gentle leg softening while mounted.
instructions:
Allow one leg at a time to shake or quiver gently without losing contact.
Keep movements small and safe.
Notice release of tension through your hips and pelvis.
evidence_base: TRE trauma release exercises adapted for mounted safety.

name: Glute Release to Seat Deepening
description: Releases glutes to improve seat depth and reduce bouncing or gripping.
instructions:
Notice if your glutes feel tight or clenched.
On each exhale, allow them to relax downward.
Observe how your horse's back responds to a deeper seat.
evidence_base: Somatic tension release; rider seat biomechanics.

name: Internal Temperature Check
description: Enhances interoception by noticing internal sensations of warmth, coolness, or temperature shifts.
instructions:
Notice internal sensations such as warmth in your chest or coolness in your hands.
Name each sensation without judging it.
Ride one lap while maintaining internal awareness.
evidence_base: Interoceptive awareness and somatic mindfulness.

name: Sensation Naming (Tight, Warm, Buzzing)
description: Names sensations to reduce emotional overwhelm and increase regulation.
instructions:
Notice a sensation such as tightness, warmth, or buzzing.
Name it simply without judgment.
Stay with the sensation for one breath before shifting focus.
evidence_base: Somatic experiencing and mindfulness naming practices.

name: Five Percent Softer Rule
description: Asks the rider to soften their body by only 5%, preserving stability while reducing tension.
instructions:
Choose one body area (jaw, shoulders, hands, thighs).
Soften that area by just 5%, not more.
Ride one lap and observe changes in your horse.
evidence_base: Somatic micro-softening and nervous system down-regulation.

name: Pressure Mapping Grip Awareness
description: Raises awareness of where the rider is gripping unnecessarily.
instructions:
Scan your body for any gripping: thighs, glutes, hands, arms.
Release one gripping area by a small amount.
Repeat for each area as needed.
evidence_base: Somatic awareness and pressure mapping research.

name: Heavy Seat Bones Grounder
description: Helps the rider deepen into the saddle for stability and calm.
instructions:
Imagine your seat bones dropping heavily into the saddle.
Allow gravity to create stable contact.
Maintain soft legs while doing so.
evidence_base: Somatic grounding principles; equitation seat training.

name: Breath and Seat Integration
description: Coordinates breath with seat movement to enhance unity with the horse.
instructions:
On each inhale, feel your pelvis rise with your horse's movement.
On each exhale, allow your seat to deepen.
Maintain integration for several cycles.
evidence_base: Somatic breath-seat integration work.

name: Pelvis–Hip–Knee Line Releasing
description: Releases the pelvis-hip-knee line to improve suppleness and reduce gripping.
instructions:
Notice the line from your pelvis to your knee on each side.
Soften or lengthen through the line on the exhale.
Switch sides and maintain symmetry.
evidence_base: Somatic line release and rider alignment.

name: Alternating Shoulder Tapping
description: Bilateral shoulder tapping to stimulate both brain hemispheres and support emotional regulation.
instructions:
With your horse in a calm walk, hold the reins in one hand if safe or loop them briefly.
Use your right hand to gently tap your left shoulder a few times, then your left hand to tap your right shoulder, alternating right-left-right-left.
Keep the tapping soft and rhythmic while breathing slowly.
Continue for 20–40 taps, then return your hands to the reins and notice any sense of calm or clarity.
evidence_base: Bilateral stimulation methods used in EMDR and trauma-informed therapies.

name: Bilateral Seat Bone Shift
description: Subtle alternating weight shifts in the seat, functioning like bilateral stimulation through the pelvis.
instructions:
At the walk, slightly increase weight onto your left seat bone, then your right, in a slow alternating rhythm.
Keep the movement small and synchronized with your horse's stride.
Continue for one or two long sides of the arena and observe your horse's response.
evidence_base: Somatic bilateral movement; co-regulation via movement rhythms.

name: Reset Tapping Before Transition
description: Brief bilateral tapping to reset the nervous system immediately before a gait or movement transition.
instructions:
Before asking for a transition, briefly tap both thighs with your hands in an alternating pattern for a few seconds.
Take one slow, deep breath while tapping.
Stop tapping, pick up your reins as needed, and cue the transition from a calmer state.
evidence_base: Bilateral pre-performance reset strategies.

name: Tapping Into Focus (Pre-Jump or Test Prep)
description: Helps riders transition from scattered attention into clear focus before a jump or test movement.
instructions:
At the walk or halt before a line or movement, tap alternately on your thighs or shoulders.
Silently say: Focus here, now, on this next line.
Stop tapping, take one slow inhale and exhale, and ride the movement with your attention on specific cues (line, rhythm, hands, and seat).
evidence_base: Performance tapping combined with attentional cueing.

name: Pre-Test Nerves EFT
description: Short tapping protocol focusing on anticipatory nervousness before a dressage test or pattern.
instructions:
While mounted and waiting for your turn, tap through a few points such as side of hand, collarbone, and wrist.
Name your feelings honestly: I feel shaky, I am afraid of messing up, I want to do well.
Finish by tapping your collarbone while saying: I can ride the best I can with the horse I have today.
Take one long exhale and prepare to enter at A or start the pattern.
evidence_base: EFT for performance anxiety; anticipatory stress protocols.

name: Tap for After-Spook Reset
description: Helps the rider's nervous system recover after a horse spook or sudden event.
instructions:
Once the horse is back under control and walking safely, begin light tapping on your thighs or shoulders.
Acknowledge: That scared me, and I handled it enough to still be here.
Pair tapping with long exhales until your heart rate begins to slow.
Decide calmly whether to continue the session or take a break.
evidence_base: Post-incident grounding; bilateral stimulation for acute stress.

name: Body Scan in Motion (Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction)
instructions: Notice seat bones, thigh tension, jaw, shoulders. Release tension deliberately into the saddle.

name: Peripheral Vision Expansion (Nervous System Regulation)
instructions: Widen your gaze to include arena walls, sky line, etc.

name: Somatic Swallow Release
instructions: Inhale. Slow conscious swallow. Soft exhale.

name: 3-Point Contact Grounding
instructions: Bring attention to 3 body-horse contact points: Seat bones, Inner calf, Reins through fingers. Exhale slowly.

name: Micro-Shake Release
instructions: While walking, allow one leg to shake out briefly. Or shake out wrists.

name: The 'Downward Breath' (Polyvagal Down-Regulation)
instructions: Inhale up the spine. Exhale down into the saddle.

name: Breath-Per-Stride Synchronization
description: Synchronizes breath rhythm to horse footfalls to increase stability and focus.
instructions:
At the walk, match your inhale to 2–3 steps and exhale to 3–4 steps.
Keep your breathing smooth, allowing your pelvis to follow the horse.
Ride one arena lap maintaining this rhythm.
evidence_base: Sports synchrony and paced-breathing research.

name: Noticing Micro-Tension (2 Percent Release)
description: Mindfulness practice aimed at identifying and reducing tiny amounts of tension in the rider's body.
instructions:
Scan for tiny tension areas in shoulders, jaw, thighs, or hands.
Release tension by only 2%, keeping movements small and safe.
Notice your horse soften in response.
evidence_base: Somatic mindfulness, micro-relaxation research, horse-rider tension studies.

name: Rider Thought Labeling: 'This is a thought'
description: Cognitive defusion practice to separate thoughts from actions while riding.
instructions:
Notice any stressful or distracting thought.
Label it: 'This is a thought, not a fact.'
Return focus to your horse's movement.
evidence_base: ACT cognitive defusion, mindfulness-based cognitive therapy.

name: Observation Without Judgment (MBSR)
description: Encourages non-judgmental awareness of internal and external experience while mounted.
instructions:
Notice sensations, posture, and horse behavior without assigning meaning.
Practice accepting what is happening rather than correcting immediately.
Stay with non-judgment for one arena long side.
evidence_base: Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (MBSR).

name: Wrist Shake-Out
description: Releases hand and wrist tension that can travel through the reins to the horse.
instructions:
Shake out one wrist at a time softly while keeping a neutral rein with the other hand.
Switch sides.
Return to the reins with softened fingers.
evidence_base: Somatic tension release, hand relaxation in fine-motor sports.

name: Neck Softening Within Safety
description: Releases neck tension without compromising stability or balance.
instructions:
Gently turn your head left and right within a safe range.
Drop your chin slightly, softening the back of your neck.
Keep shoulders soft while doing this.
evidence_base: Somatic neck release and posture regulation.

name: Thigh Softening Scan
description: Releases gripping in the thighs to increase horse-rider harmony.
instructions:
Scan through both thighs to identify gripping or tension.
Release each thigh by 5–10% on every exhale.
Notice how your horse's back and stride respond.
evidence_base: Somatic release techniques; rider posture research.

name: Lower Back Melt
description: Relaxes the lower back to reduce bracing and improve balance.
instructions:
Imagine your lower back melting downward like warm wax.
Allow the movement of your horse to gently mobilize your spine.
Maintain softness for several breaths.
evidence_base: Somatic lumbar release and mobility work.

name: Somatic Allowing Practice
description: Encourages the body to allow sensations without resisting them, reducing fight-or-flight escalation.
instructions:
Notice a sensation or emotion arising in your body.
Say internally: "I can allow this sensation to be here."
Breathe slowly and observe how the sensation shifts.
evidence_base: Somatic experiencing; acceptance-based emotion regulation.

name: Soft Spine Visualization
description: Encourages a flexible, responsive spine to reduce bracing.
instructions:
Visualize your spine as a flexible chain rather than a stiff rod.
Let it respond fluidly to your horse's movement.
Hold softness for one arena long side.
evidence_base: Somatic imagery; Feldenkrais-based mobility.

name: Hand Karate Chop Tapping
description: Tapping on the side of the hand (karate chop point) paired with a set-up statement to reduce distress.
instructions:
While your horse walks quietly, bring one hand to the side of the other hand (the karate chop edge).
Tap gently on the side of your hand with two or three fingers in a steady rhythm.
Optionally repeat a phrase such as: Even though I feel anxious right now, I am doing the best I can.
Continue for 30–60 seconds, then return to normal reins and notice your nervous system level.
evidence_base: EFT set-up protocol; cognitive and somatic integration for distress tolerance.

name: Anxiety Set-Up Statement Tapping
description: Uses a set-up statement plus tapping to acknowledge anxiety and build self-acceptance.
instructions:
While your horse is calmly walking, choose a tapping point such as the side of your hand or collarbone.
Tap gently and say three times (out loud or silently): Even though I feel anxious right now, I accept that this is how I feel and I am trying my best.
Continue tapping on that point or move through other points as you ride (collarbone, chest, wrist).
Notice changes in intensity of anxiety from 0–10.
evidence_base: EFT treatment protocols for anxiety; acceptance-based approaches.

name: Confidence Set-Up Statement Tapping
description: Pairs tapping with a confidence-building set-up phrase to shift self-belief before or during a ride.
instructions:
Select a tapping point (for example, collarbone or side of hand) while your horse walks.
Tap and repeat: Even though part of me doubts myself, I am learning and I choose to ride with calm confidence.
Continue tapping and repeating the phrase for 6–10 breaths.
Return to normal reins and test how it feels to ride from this updated mindset.
evidence_base: EFT with positive cognitive restructuring for confidence.

name: Right–Left Rein Finger Tapping
description: Tiny bilateral tapping using fingers on the reins to calm the nervous system without dropping contact.
instructions:
At the walk, gently tap your right fingers on the rein, then your left fingers, alternating rhythmically.
Keep the taps very small so you do not disturb your horse's mouth.
Continue for 20–30 seconds while breathing evenly.
evidence_base: Discrete bilateral stimulation adapted for mounted use.

name: Eye-Movement Bilateral Sweep
description: Uses slow left-right eye movements to stimulate bilateral processing while mounted.
instructions:
While riding at a calm walk, choose two safe visual points in your environment—one to your left and one to your right.
Slowly move your eyes from left point to right point and back again, without turning your head drastically.
Repeat the sweep several times while breathing slowly.
Return to a neutral forward gaze.
evidence_base: EMDR-style bilateral eye movement adapted for in-saddle use.

name: Shoulder-to-Hip Bilateral Scan
description: Involves gentle touch or tapping from shoulder to opposite hip in alternation, supporting cross-body integration.
instructions:
Slide one hand briefly along the front of your body from left shoulder toward right hip, then return to the reins.
Repeat on the other side from right shoulder toward left hip.
Keep movements small and deliberate so as not to disturb your horse.
Continue alternating sides for 30–60 seconds.
evidence_base: Cross-lateral bilateral stimulation; somatic integration methods.

name: Power Phrase plus Tap
description: Pairs a chosen power phrase with tapping to embody a confident riding identity.
instructions:
Choose a phrase like I ride with clarity or I am a calm, capable rider.
Tap gently on your chest or thighs while repeating the phrase in time with your breath.
Continue for 45–60 seconds, then ride a simple line or figure focusing on that identity.
evidence_base: EFT and identity-based behavior change research.

name: Performance Identity Reset Tapping
description: Resets identity from scared or stuck rider to curious learner or calm athlete.
instructions:
Tap on a chosen point (collarbone or hand) while saying: Even though part of me feels like a bad rider, I am choosing to be a learning athlete.
Repeat for several tapping rounds, allowing the new identity phrase to settle in.
Continue riding with that identity in mind, focusing on process instead of perfection.
evidence_base: EFT combined with identity-based cognitive reframing.

name: Visualization plus Tap Combo
description: Combines positive ride visualization with tapping to strengthen neural pathways for success.
instructions:
At a walk or halt, begin gentle tapping on your thighs or collarbone.
Visualize yourself riding a line, test, or exercise calmly and effectively.
Feel the successful ride in your body while you tap.
Stop tapping, then ride a simplified version of what you visualized.
evidence_base: Sports imagery plus bilateral stimulation for performance.

name: Tap While Relaxing Jaw
description: Targets jaw tension while tapping to release upper-body bracing and worry.
instructions:
Begin gentle bilateral tapping on your thighs or shoulders.
At the same time, let your jaw soften and your tongue rest on the floor of your mouth.
Maintain tapping for 30–60 seconds as jaw tension melts.
Return to normal riding focus and observe your horse's response.
evidence_base: Somatic jaw release plus bilateral stimulation.

name: Grounding Statement plus Bilateral Tap
description: Combines bilateral tapping with a simple grounding sentence to stabilize the rider and support the horse.
instructions:
Tap alternately on your thighs or shoulders while your horse walks calmly.
Choose one grounding statement such as: One breath, one stride, one step at a time.
Repeat the statement in time with your tapping for 45–60 seconds.
Stop tapping and keep the grounding statement in mind as you continue riding.
evidence_base: Combined grounding statements and bilateral stimulation for emotional regulation.

name: The 'Safe Seat' Reset (Somatic Trauma Model + Polyvagal)
instructions: Deepen your breath. Let your weight drop into thighs + stirrups. Feel the horse's back move under you.

name: Pelvic 'Float' Reset
instructions: At walk, allow your pelvis to follow the horse's movement. Visualize the motion as a figure-8. Let your seat bones get heavy.

name: Box Breath (Modified for Riding)
instructions: Inhale 4. Hold 2. Exhale 6. Hold 2.

name: Side-Body Stretch Breath
instructions: Inhale and lengthen right side. Exhale soften. Repeat on left.

name: Morning Ride Preparation
description: Start your riding day centered and positive
instructions: Karate Chop: "Even though I don't know what today will bring, I welcome it with an open heart." Tap through: Eyebrow - "Today is a new beginning..." Side of Eye - "I am open to learning..." Under Eye - "I feel grateful for my horse..." Under Nose - "We communicate with trust..." Under Mouth - "I ride with intention..." Collarbone - "My mind is clear..." Under Arm - "My body is ready..." Top of Head - "This will be a good day." Set your positive intention.

name: Long Exhale Relaxation Breath
description: Uses elongated exhalation to shift the nervous system toward parasympathetic calm.
instructions:
At the walk, inhale normally.
Make your exhale twice as long as the inhale, letting your shoulders drop.
Continue for several cycles, noticing changes in your horse's stride.
evidence_base: Respiratory sinus arrhythmia research; breathwork for autonomic down-regulation.

name: Breath Into Belt Line
description: Expands diaphragm and lowers tension by breathing 360° around the waistline.
instructions:
At the walk, breathe low into your belly and around your waist.
Feel the belt-line expand evenly.
Release on the exhale and soften your seat.
evidence_base: Diaphragmatic breathing research; somatic therapy.

name: Seat-Bone Awareness Tracking
description: Mindfulness exercise focusing on awareness of the rider's seat bones and how they move with the horse.
instructions:
At the walk, notice each seat bone independently.
Observe how they rise, lower, and follow the swing of the horse's back.
Maintain awareness for one arena lap.
evidence_base: Somatic mindfulness, body-awareness research, rider biomechanics studies.

name: Body-to-Horse Synchrony Check
description: Enhances rider-horse synchrony by focusing attention on shared movement rhythm.
instructions:
Allow your body to follow your horse's movement without bracing.
Notice where movement flows smoothly and where it feels blocked.
Soften tension and rejoin your horse's rhythm.
evidence_base: Co-regulation research, equine biomechanics, mindfulness in motion.

name: Noticing Horse Micro-Cues
description: Enhances horse-rider communication by noticing subtle signals such as breath changes or ear flicks.
instructions:
Observe your horse's small signals: breath, ears, neck, stride.
Notice patterns without reacting right away.
Stay curious, not critical, about what your horse communicates.
evidence_base: Equine behavior science, mindfulness-based observation.

name: Vagal Hum Exhale
description: Uses humming on the exhale to stimulate the vagus nerve and calm both horse and rider.
instructions:
Take a slow inhale through your nose.
Exhale with a gentle hum, letting the vibration soften your chest and throat.
Repeat for 4–6 cycles and observe your horse's breathing or ear position.
evidence_base: Vagal toning research, breath-based nervous-system regulation.

name: Pelvic Float Reset
description: Encourages the pelvis to follow the horse's movement in a fluid, unbraced pattern.
instructions:
Imagine your pelvis floating like a buoy on water as your horse moves.
Let your seat move freely without gripping or controlling.
Allow small figure-8 motions to emerge naturally.
evidence_base: Feldenkrais-inspired somatic mobility; rider biomechanics.

name: Polyvagal Anchor: Breath Down Spine
description: Visualization of breath flowing down the spine to engage dorsal and ventral vagal regulation.
instructions:
Inhale and imagine the breath traveling from the top of your spine downward.
Exhale and imagine it grounding through your pelvis into the saddle.
Repeat slowly for 6–10 breaths.
evidence_base: Polyvagal theory; somatic breath-based grounding.

name: Sternum Drop Reset
description: Softening the sternum releases bracing in the upper chest and improves breathing efficiency.
instructions: Soften the sternum just 2%. Let shoulders widen instead of lift. Breathe gently.
evidence_base: Somatic postural work; trauma-informed chest release.

name: Side-Body Release
description: Releases bracing in the rider's lateral line to increase symmetry and softness.
instructions:
Gently lengthen through the right side of your body for one breath.
Then lengthen the left side.
Return to neutral and notice improved softness and mobility.
evidence_base: Somatic lateral-line release; body mapping.

name: Mirror Neuron Relaxation
description: Uses calm visual focus to encourage the rider's body to soften through mirror-neuron pathways.
instructions:
Focus on something calm and steady in the environment (tree, wall, horizon).
Let your body mimic the stillness you are observing.
Ride slowly while maintaining this soft gaze.
evidence_base: Mirror-neuron system research, equine-assisted therapy observations.

name: Somatic Sigh Release
description: Uses a gentle sigh to discharge upper-body tension.
instructions:
Take a soft inhale through your nose.
Exhale with a gentle sigh through your mouth.
Repeat 3–4 times without collapsing your posture.
evidence_base: Somatic tension release and breath research.

name: Hand Open–Close Release
description: Opens and closes fingers gently to release hand bracing and rein tension.
instructions:
Open your fingers wide for a moment without losing rein feel.
Close gently, then reopen softly.
Repeat several times while keeping wrists relaxed.
evidence_base: Somatic hand release; neuromuscular relaxation.

name: Internal Energy Direction Downward
description: Directs internal energy downward through the seat to create stability and security.
instructions:
Imagine energy flowing downward from your chest through your seat.
Let gravity assist the downward flow until your seat deepens.
Stay connected with slow breathing.
evidence_base: Grounding and somatic energy-direction practices.

name: Feel Horse Back Movement
description: Trains the rider to sense the vertical and lateral movement of the horse's back.
instructions:
Focus on how your horse's back lifts and swings under you.
Follow the movement without bracing or forcing.
Notice any areas where your body stiffens and soften them.
evidence_base: Equine proprioception awareness; somatic seat training.

name: Co-Release Rider Exhale → Horse Softens
description: Uses the rider's exhale as a cue for the horse to soften or release tension.
instructions:
On each slow exhale, soften your entire torso.
Notice if your horse drops its head, blows out, or relaxes.
Continue pattern for one arena lap.
evidence_base: Co-regulation research; equine behavioral mirroring.

name: Bilateral Thigh Tapping
description: Tapping alternately on each thigh to ground the rider and calm the nervous system.
instructions:
At the walk, place one hand lightly on each thigh.
Tap alternately left, right, left, right on your thighs in a gentle, steady rhythm.
Pair the tapping with slower breathing and a neutral focus on your horse's movement.
Continue for 30–60 seconds, then rest your hands back on the reins.
evidence_base: Bilateral tapping used in EMDR, DBT, and somatic trauma protocols.

name: Light Chest Tapping
description: Soft tapping in the upper chest area to help release emotional pressure and support calmer breathing.
instructions:
Ensure your horse is relaxed at the walk or halt.
Use fingertips to gently tap in the center of your upper chest, avoiding any painful areas.
Coordinate the tapping with slow inhales and long exhales.
Continue for 30–45 seconds, then notice any softening in your chest and shoulders.
evidence_base: EFT tapping locations; somatic chest release for anxiety.

name: Flow-State Tapping
description: Tapping designed to support a focused, in-the-zone riding state by clearing distractions.
instructions:
With your horse at a walk, tap lightly on your collarbone or thighs in a steady bilateral rhythm.
Repeat a brief phrase such as: Here, now, with my horse.
Maintain tapping and phrase repetition for 45–60 seconds, then ride a simple pattern focusing on feel and rhythm.
evidence_base: Bilateral stimulation and sports flow-state research.

name: Pre-Competition EFT Sequence
description: A short tapping sequence used before entering the ring to manage nerves and steady focus.
instructions:
While walking or halted near the arena, tap through a brief sequence: side of hand, collarbone, chest, wrist.
At each point, name what you feel (for example: nervous, tight, worried) and acknowledge your effort.
Finish by tapping at the collarbone while repeating a calm phrase such as: I know my horse, I know my ride.
Take one last slow breath and ride your entry line.
evidence_base: EFT protocols applied to sports performance anxiety.

name: Right–Left Thigh Alternating
description: Alternating taps on each thigh for grounding and bilateral neural activation.
instructions:
Place one hand near each thigh while your horse walks.
Tap left thigh, then right thigh, in a slow, even rhythm.
Continue tapping for 30–60 seconds, then place your hands back on the reins and feel your seat deepening into the saddle.
evidence_base: Bilateral stimulation, grounding techniques for trauma.

name: Foot Pressure Bilateral Switching
description: Alternating heel or stirrup pressure to create bilateral grounding through the legs.
instructions:
Gently press more weight into your left stirrup, then your right, alternating in a calm rhythm.
Avoid jabbing or gripping; keep the switches smooth.
Continue for 30–60 seconds, then return to even weight.
evidence_base: Grounding via proprioceptive pressure and bilateral stimulation.

name: Tapping to Horse's Walk Rhythm
description: Matches bilateral tapping to the 4-beat walk rhythm to enhance co-regulation.
instructions:
Notice the four-beat rhythm of your horse's walk.
Tap alternately on your thighs or shoulders in time with the steps.
Continue for one arena lap while keeping your breathing slow and steady.
evidence_base: Rhythmic entrainment research; bilateral stimulation in motion.

name: Alternate Rein Slide Touch
description: A discrete bilateral technique where the rider alternately slides fingers along each rein.
instructions:
At the walk, gently slide the fingers of your right hand a few centimeters along the rein, then return.
Then slide the fingers of your left hand along the rein, alternating right and left.
Keep the contact soft and consistent so the horse is not startled.
Continue for 20–40 seconds while breathing slowly.
evidence_base: Discrete bilateral stimulation; sensory grounding.

name: Tap plus Long Exhale
description: Pairs bilateral tapping with prolonged exhalation to quickly down-regulate the nervous system.
instructions:
Tap alternately on your thighs or shoulders in a slow rhythm.
Inhale normally, then exhale for a slow count of six or longer as you keep tapping.
Repeat the long exhale plus tapping for 4–6 breaths.
evidence_base: Breath-based vagal regulation plus bilateral stimulation.

name: Tap While Engaging Seat Rhythm
description: Uses rhythmic seat motion plus tapping for full-body regulation.
instructions:
At the walk, let your seat move fluidly with your horse's back.
Lightly tap alternately on your thighs in time with the stride.
Continue for one arena lap, focusing on the combined rhythm of seat, horse, and tapping.
evidence_base: Rhythmic regulation; bilateral entrainment strategies.

name: Tap plus Soft Gaze
description: Supports a soft, wide visual field while using bilateral tapping to reduce hyperfocus or tunnel vision.
instructions:
Soften your eyes and allow your gaze to widen so you see more of the arena.
Tap alternately on your thighs or shoulders as you hold this soft, wide focus.
Continue for one arena lap, then stop tapping and keep the soft gaze as you ride.
evidence_base: Visual field regulation plus bilateral tapping for anxiety.

name: Breath-Sync Regulation (Somatic + HRV Training)
instructions: Inhale for 3 steps → exhale for 4–5 steps. Let the exhale 'melt' into the saddle.

name: Cognitive Grounding Through Sensory Anchors (CBT)
instructions: Identify 3 things you see, 2 things you physically feel in the saddle, 1 sound in the environment.

name: Thought Labelling + Releasing (CBT + ACT)
instructions: Identify the thought → name it → separate from it. For example: 'That's an anxious thought.' 'I don't have to act on it.'

name: Rib Cage Expansion Breath
instructions: Inhale sideways into the ribs. Feel ribs widen into thighs. Exhale to soften chest + sternum.

name: Breath-Per-Stride Sync
instructions: Pick a rhythm: Inhale 2 strides / Exhale 3 strides. Or inhale 3 / exhale 4 for anxious riders.

name: Low & Slow Belly Breath
instructions: One hand on your thigh. Send breath into the lower belly. Exhale downwards through seat.

name: Gentle 'Hum' Exhale
instructions: Exhale with a low hum.

name: Fear of Falling Reset
description: Release fear and build confidence after a fall or scary moment
instructions: Begin at the Karate Chop point, tapping while saying: "Even though I have this fear of falling, I am safe right now." Move through the points: Eyebrow - "This fear in my body..." Side of Eye - "This worry about falling..." Under Eye - "Feeling unsafe..." Under Nose - "This fear..." Under Mouth - "I choose to feel grounded..." Collarbone - "I am learning and growing..." Under Arm - "My body knows how to balance..." Top of Head - "I trust myself and my horse." Repeat until fear diminishes.

name: Competition Day Calm
description: Reduce performance anxiety before showing
instructions: Karate Chop setup: "Even though I feel pressure to perform, I choose to enjoy this moment with my horse." Tap through the sequence: Eyebrow - "This performance pressure..." Side of Eye - "This need to be perfect..." Under Eye - "Worrying about what others think..." Under Nose - "This anxiety about mistakes..." Under Mouth - "I release this pressure..." Collarbone - "I am prepared..." Under Arm - "My horse and I are partners..." Top of Head - "We ride with joy and confidence." 2-3 rounds.

name: Quick Confidence Boost
description: Fast tapping sequence to build confidence before any challenge
instructions: Rapid tapping sequence - spend just 10 seconds on each point. Karate Chop: "I am capable and strong." Eyebrow: "I trust myself." Side of Eye: "I am confident." Under Eye: "I feel safe." Under Nose: "I am prepared." Under Mouth: "I believe in myself." Collarbone: "My horse trusts me." Under Arm: "We work together." Top of Head: "I am ready." Repeat 2 times quickly.

name: Post-Ride Processing
description: Release stress and integrate lessons after a difficult ride
instructions: Karate Chop: "Even though that ride was challenging, I honor my effort and my horse's effort." Gently tap through points: Eyebrow - "Whatever happened today..." Side of Eye - "Any disappointment I feel..." Under Eye - "Any frustration..." Under Nose - "I acknowledge these feelings..." Under Mouth - "I learned something today..." Collarbone - "I am growing as a rider..." Under Arm - "Tomorrow is a new day..." Top of Head - "I release this and move forward with grace." Take deep breaths between rounds.

name: Trauma Release for Horse & Rider
description: Gentle tapping to process past scary experiences
instructions: This is for processing past events, not current danger. Karate Chop: "Even though that scary thing happened, I am safe now." Very gently tap: Eyebrow - "That memory..." Side of Eye - "How it made me feel..." Under Eye - "The fear that stayed with me..." Under Nose - "It's in the past now..." Under Mouth - "I am safe in this moment..." Collarbone - "My body can release this..." Under Arm - "I choose peace..." Top of Head - "I am healing." Go slowly, breathe deeply. Repeat as needed over several sessions.

name: HRV Coherence Breath (Inhale 4, Exhale 6)
description: Creates heart-rate variability coherence by lengthening the exhale and synchronizing with horse movement.
instructions:
Place your horse in a relaxed walk or quiet halt.
Inhale softly through your nose for 4 counts, then exhale gently for 6 counts.
Repeat for 6–10 breath cycles while monitoring your horse's relaxation.
evidence_base: HeartMath HRV coherence protocols, autonomic regulation research.

name: Co-Regulating with Horse Movement Breath
description: Pairs breath with the horse's natural back swing to regulate tension.
instructions:
Feel your horse's back move under your seat.
Inhale as your pelvis rises and exhale as it settles.
Stay with the movement for 10–12 cycles.
evidence_base: Co-regulation and animal-assisted nervous-system synchronization research.

name: Double-Length Exhale (4:8)
description: Regulates the nervous system by extending the exhale to twice the length of the inhale.
instructions:
Inhale for 4 counts.
Exhale softly for 8 counts without pushing air out.
Continue for 5–7 cycles.
evidence_base: Breathwork down-regulation studies (Huberman, RSA modulation).

name: Exhale Seat-Softening Breath
description: Softens the seat and thighs during the exhale to improve freedom of horse movement.
instructions:
As you exhale, let your seat and thighs grow heavier and softer.
Continue for 8-10 breath cycles while maintaining contact with your horse.
Notice how your horse responds to the relaxation.
evidence_base: Somatic release and rider tension research.

name: Slow Blink Safety Signal
description: Uses slow, soft eye blinks to cue the nervous system and the horse that there is no threat.
instructions:
Relax your eyes and close them softly for a brief moment.
Blink slowly several times, keeping your jaw soft.
Pair the blinks with long exhales.
evidence_base: Polyvagal safety cues; equine calming-signal research.

name: Micro-Movement Spine Wave
description: Small spinal undulation to release rigidity and improve harmony with horse movement.
instructions:
Gently create a wave-like motion up your spine, matching your horse's movement.
Keep the wave subtle and fluid.
Repeat for one long side of the arena.
evidence_base: Feldenkrais spinal mobility techniques.

name: Heartbeat Awareness
description: Builds interoceptive awareness by noticing the pulse or heartbeat while riding.
instructions:
Bring your attention to your heartbeat or pulse sensations.
Notice if the rhythm changes as you breathe and ride.
Pair heartbeat awareness with slow exhales.
evidence_base: Interoception research; somatic emotional regulation.

name: Breath-to-Tension Mapping
description: Maps where breath flows and where it does not, revealing areas of hidden tension.
instructions:
Notice which parts of your body move with your breath.
Notice which parts feel still or blocked.
Direct breath gently toward blocked areas without forcing.
evidence_base: Breath mapping and somatic therapy research.

name: Expand vs Contract Body Check
description: Identifies whether the body is bracing (contracted) or softening (expanded).
instructions:
Ask yourself: "Is my body expanding or contracting right now?"
If contracting, soften one small area such as your jaw or ribs.
Ride one long side noticing the shift.
evidence_base: Somatic contraction/expansion patterns in trauma and stress.

name: Micro-Postural Adjustments
description: Uses tiny alignment shifts to break out of rigid posture cycles.
instructions:
Shift your posture by just 2–5%: soften your shoulders, lengthen your spine, or adjust your pelvis.
Keep the adjustments tiny to stay balanced.
Repeat small resets every few strides.
evidence_base: Micro-movement somatic regulation.

name: Synchronize with Horse Swing
description: Enhances rider-horse harmony by matching the swing of the horse's rib cage and back.
instructions:
Feel your horse's ribcage swing left and right under your seat.
Allow your hips and lower back to follow the movement.
Stay soft and rhythmically connected for one arena lap.
evidence_base: Equine biomechanics; entrainment research.

name: Seat Rhythm Calibration
description: Improves seat timing and balance by calibrating movement against the horse's gait rhythm.
instructions:
Sit quietly at the walk and tune into the rhythm of the gait.
Match your seat movement precisely with each step.
Notice increased stability and relaxation.
evidence_base: Rider biomechanics; somatic rhythm entrainment.

name: Somatic Mirroring Exercise
description: Encourages the rider to mirror the horse's relaxation patterns to create mutual regulation.
instructions:
Observe your horse's breathing, rhythm, and posture.
Mirror any softening or relaxing gesture your horse shows.
Allow mutual regulation to develop between you.
evidence_base: Co-regulation and mirror neuron research.

name: Aid from Soft Body, Not Tension
description: Redirects effort from braced muscles into soft, effective rider aids.
instructions:
Before giving an aid, soften your torso and release gripping.
Give the aid from softness rather than force.
Notice your horse's acceptance of the aid.
evidence_base: Equitation science; somatic movement efficiency.

name: Collarbone Tapping
description: On-horse EFT-style tapping on the collarbone points to reduce anxiety and reset the nervous system.
instructions:
Ensure your horse is walking calmly on a loose or neutral rein in a safe environment.
With one or two fingers, gently tap on the soft area just below your collarbone on one side, keeping the tapping light and rhythmic.
Breathe slowly as you tap and, if helpful, name what you are feeling (for example, nervous, tight, overwhelmed).
Continue for 30–60 seconds, then return both hands to the reins and notice any change in your body and your horse.
evidence_base: Emotional Freedom Techniques (EFT) research for anxiety and stress reduction; bilateral stimulation in trauma-focused therapies.

name: Wrist Tapping Sequence
description: Gentle tapping on the inside of the wrist to reduce activation before or during a ride.
instructions:
With your horse calmly walking, bring one hand toward the inside of the opposite wrist.
Tap gently on the inside of the wrist where a pulse might be felt.
Breathe in for a slow count of four and out for a slow count of six as you tap.
Repeat for 6–10 breaths, then return your hand to the reins.
evidence_base: Acupressure-informed tapping points; EFT and anxiety reduction literature.

name: Rhythmic Belly Breath and Tap
description: Combines belly breathing with tapping to support deep regulation.
instructions:
Place one hand lightly on your lower belly and the other hand on your thigh.
As you breathe into your belly, gently tap the hand on your thigh in rhythm with your breath.
Continue for 6–10 breaths, then ride on and notice changes in your body tone.
evidence_base: Combined breathwork and bilateral tapping interventions.

name: Bilateral Breath Sides Awareness
description: Focuses on breathing alternately into left and right sides of the ribcage for bilateral regulation.
instructions:
As you inhale, imagine breathing more into the left side of your ribs; as you exhale, relax.
On the next inhale, imagine breathing more into the right side.
Alternate left and right for 8–10 breaths while walking your horse.
evidence_base: Somatic breathwork; lateralized interoception practices.

name: Tapping Release for Overthinking
description: Targets mental loops and overanalysis by combining tapping with cognitive defusion phrases.
instructions:
While your horse walks quietly, tap on your collarbone or thighs.
Repeat phrases such as: These are just thoughts, not commands or My brain is busy, but my body can stay calm.
Continue tapping and repeating for 1–2 minutes, then ride a simple pattern focusing only on feel.
evidence_base: EFT plus ACT cognitive defusion strategies.

name: Tapping for Letting Go of Mistakes
description: Supports emotional recovery after small riding mistakes so they do not derail the session.
instructions:
After a mistake or rough moment, keep your horse moving safely at the walk.
Tap gently on your chest or collarbone and say: I notice that happened, and I can learn without beating myself up.
Continue tapping for 30–60 seconds, then reset and ride the line again if appropriate.
evidence_base: Self-compassion research; EFT for shame and performance recovery.

name: Confidence Access Tapping
description: Helps riders reconnect with a previous memory of competence and calm while tapping.
instructions:
Begin gentle tapping on your collarbone or wrist.
Recall a time you felt confident and effective in the saddle or in another area of life.
As you tap, bring that memory into your body: posture, breath, and feeling.
Ride on from that memory state and notice any change.
evidence_base: Resource tapping; resourcing techniques in trauma therapy and sports psych.

name: Course Memory Tapping
description: Uses tapping to support memory and calm when remembering a jump course or pattern.
instructions:
While mounted and walking, tap alternately on your thighs or shoulders.
Silently rehearse your course or pattern: fence numbers, lines, letters, or movements.
If anxious thoughts appear, acknowledge them and return to calmly reviewing the pattern while tapping.
evidence_base: Bilateral stimulation plus mental rehearsal in sport psychology.

name: Tap to Reduce Hypervigilance
description: Helps riders who are constantly scanning for danger bring their nervous system into a more balanced state.
instructions:
Begin bilateral tapping on your thighs, shoulders, or wrists while your horse walks in a safe area.
Acknowledge: My body is on high alert, and I am not in immediate danger right now.
Let your eyes briefly scan the environment once, then bring your gaze to a calm focal point.
Continue tapping until your activation feels one or two points lower on a 0–10 scale.
evidence_base: Trauma-informed bilateral stimulation for hyperarousal.

name: Tap to Anchor to Present
description: Uses tapping plus present-focused cues to interrupt time-traveling into past falls or future fears.
instructions:
Tap alternately on your thighs or shoulders.
Say quietly: Right now I am here, on this horse, in this arena.
Add simple details: It is [today's weather], I can feel the saddle, I hear hoofbeats.
Continue for 30–60 seconds until the present feels more real than old memories or imagined disasters.
evidence_base: Grounding and orientation techniques plus bilateral stimulation.

name: I Am Safe Tapping Loop
description: Reinforces safety messages while tapping when there is no actual immediate threat.
instructions:
Begin tapping alternately on your collarbone or thighs.
Repeat softly: In this moment, I am safe enough to ride.
Scan your environment quickly once to confirm there is no real threat.
Continue tapping and repeating the phrase for 45–60 seconds.
evidence_base: Safety cueing in trauma therapy plus EFT techniques.

name: Tap for Freeze Response
description: Designed for riders who go into a freeze or shut-down response in the saddle.
instructions:
If you notice yourself going numb or frozen, keep your horse walking on a small, safe circle if possible.
Tap firmly but gently on your thighs or shoulders in an alternating rhythm.
Quietly say: I am here, I am in my body, I can move.
Continue until you feel even a small return of warmth, sensation, or emotion, then pair with grounding breath.
evidence_base: Bilateral stimulation for freeze and shutdown states in trauma work.

name: Dual Awareness Cue (DBT Distress Tolerance)
instructions: Say internally: 'My body is tense AND my horse is steady.'

name: Micro-Goal Cueing (Sports Psychology)
instructions: Set micro-goals like: 'Next 5 strides: steady hands.' or 'Next corner: soft seat.'

name: Interoception Check-In (Somatic + Mind-Body Integration)
instructions: Ask yourself: 'Where is tension?' 'What is my breath doing?' 'Can I soften by 5%?'

name: Co-Regulation Cue (Polyvagal + Equine Behavior Science)
instructions: Match your breathing to the horse's exhale rhythm. Feel the sway of the walk. Visualize energy flowing downward.

name: 4:8 Tension Melt Exhale
instructions: Inhale for 4. Long exhale for 8. Imagine tension draining out of your shoulders and seat.

name: 'Soft Jaw–Soft Horse' Release
instructions: Loosen your jaw. Let tongue rest on the floor of your mouth. Exhale with a tiny sigh.

name: Shoulder Blade 'Slide Down' Reset
instructions: Slide shoulder blades into back pockets. Exhale.

name: Heart-Space Breath
instructions: Inhale as if breathing into the space behind your collarbones. Exhale through the chest downward.

name: Glute/Thigh Release Scan
instructions: On exhale, check: 'Am I gripping?' Release thighs by 10%. Let seat deepen.

name: Slow Blink Reset
instructions: Inhale. Slow soft blink. Exhale.

name: 'Open Hand' Reset
instructions: Momentarily open each hand. Re-close with softness. Exhale.

name: Eye-Softening Peripheral Vision
instructions: Expand your gaze to include arena edges. Breathe slowly.

name: 90-Second Arousal Balance Reset
instructions: You are allowed to feel amped and still ride with clarity. 1) Stand or sit tall and plant your feet. 2) Inhale gently through your nose for a count of 4, noticing the expansion in your ribs and back. 3) Exhale with a soft sigh for a count of 6–8, letting your shoulders drop. 4) On each exhale, silently repeat: Steady and ready. 5) Complete 8–10 breaths, then quickly scan your body: jaw, shoulders, hands, thighs. Loosen any area still gripping. 6) Step toward your ride with the phrase: I can use this energy to focus.

name: Competition Nerves: Label and Aim
instructions: This tool channels your nervous energy instead of trying to erase it. 1) Notice your body signals (butterflies, buzzing, heat, shallow breath). 2) Say out loud or in your mind: This is my body preparing to perform. 3) Label the feeling with a helpful word: excited, charged, switched on. 4) Choose one task to aim this energy at (for example: Ride the first centerline with softness and straightness.). 5) Visualize sending the energy into that specific task instead of letting it spread everywhere.

name: Walk-the-Ring Pressure Release
instructions: Use this if you feel keyed up while waiting near the arena. 1) Walk slowly around your warm-up or a quiet space, feeling your feet roll from heel to toe. 2) On each exhale, let your arms swing a little and imagine excess pressure draining into the ground. 3) Choose a simple cue phrase such as: Breathe and ride or Soft and accurate. 4) Repeat this phrase in rhythm with your steps and breath. 5) After 2–3 minutes, pause, roll your shoulders, and imagine you and your horse stepping into a calmer bubble together.

name: Show Ring Box Breathing
instructions: Use this when you feel your heart racing before entering the ring. 1) Imagine tracing a square in your mind. 2) Inhale through your nose for 4 counts (side one of the square). 3) Hold your breath gently for 4 counts (side two). 4) Exhale slowly through pursed lips for 4 counts (side three). 5) Pause empty for 4 counts (side four). 6) Repeat this box 6–8 times, keeping your shoulders soft and your jaw unclenched. 7) When finished, take one normal breath and say: Steady body, clear mind.

name: Competition Exhale-Extend Breathing
instructions: If your breathing feels tight and high in your chest, use this reset. 1) Place one hand on your belly, one on your chest. 2) Inhale gently through your nose for 3–4 counts, letting your belly move slightly more than your chest. 3) Exhale for 6–8 counts through slightly parted lips, like fogging a mirror quietly. 4) With each exhale, picture the tension flowing out of your hands, thighs, and jaw. 5) Complete 10–12 breaths. 6) Finish by imagining sending one slow, calm breath down the reins to your horse.

name: Clear Round Mini Visualization
instructions: Use this 3-minute imagery right before you ride. 1) Close your eyes or soften your gaze. 2) Picture yourself entering the arena with shoulders soft, hands steady, and breathing smooth. 3) Run through the first 3–5 movements or jumps: see your track, feel your body staying tall and centered, and your horse responding to light aids. 4) Imagine making one small mistake and calmly correcting it, proving to your brain that you can adapt. 5) End the visualization with a clear, confident finish and a sense of quiet pride in your chest.

name: At-the-Gate Calm Start Visual
instructions: Use this while waiting at the in-gate. 1) Look at the arena and imagine a calm bubble forming around the space where you and your horse will ride. 2) See yourself walking in with a relaxed jaw, long leg, and gentle contact. 3) Picture your first transition or first turn going well: you breathe out, your horse softens, and you stay balanced. 4) Let the image play like a short movie with one key phrase such as: Soft, accurate, present. 5) Open your eyes and step into that bubble as if you are stepping into the movie you just watched.

name: Ride Your Strength Highlight
instructions: This tool uses confidence to quiet nerves. 1) Identify one strength movement or skill (for example: transitions, rhythm, or accurate lines). 2) Close your eyes and replay a memory where you rode that strength well. 3) Notice the details: your posture, your horse response, and how your body felt. 4) Now visualize bringing that exact same quality into todays ride, especially in the first third of your test or course. 5) Finish with: I know how to do this. I have done it before.

name: Competition Pre-Ride Focus 3×3
instructions: Use this to organize your mind before mounting. 1) Name 3 things that are going well today (for example: horse is warmed up, I know my pattern, I am prepared). 2) Name 3 simple ride goals (for example: breathe in the corners, soft hands, ride forward off the leg). 3) Name 3 things you will let go of (for example: the score, other riders opinions, yesterdays ride). 4) Take one slow breath after each set of three. 5) Mount or walk to the gate holding only the 3 simple ride goals.

name: Mounting Block Focus Sequence
instructions: Use the mounting block as a reset point. 1) Before you step up, pause and place one hand on your horses neck, feeling their breathing for 2–3 breaths. 2) Step onto the block and take one slow inhale, imagining your spine lengthening. 3) As you exhale, say your ride mantra (for example: Calm and clear.). 4) Mount slowly, paying attention to each movement instead of rushing. 5) Once in the saddle, check three soft points: fingers, jaw, and thighs. 6) Only then ask your horse to walk off.

name: In-Gate One-Thing Focus
instructions: When you feel overwhelmed by instructions and expectations, use this tool. 1) Ask yourself: What is the ONE thing that would help this ride most right now? (for example: ride forward, keep breathing, look ahead). 2) Say that one thing in your mind on every inhale and exhale. 3) As you enter the arena, imagine placing that one focus on the center of the ring, like a guiding star. 4) Any time your mind wanders, bring it gently back to that single focus.

name: Low Energy 5-Minute Activation
instructions: Use this when you feel flat or unmotivated before riding. 1) Set a 5-minute timer. 2) March in place or walk briskly around the barn, swinging your arms and gently rolling your shoulders. 3) Inhale through your nose for 3 counts, exhale through your mouth for 3 counts to create a light, energizing rhythm. 4) With each step, repeat a short phrase like: Waking up my body. 5) When the timer ends, pause, place a hand on your chest, and notice any increase in warmth, heartbeat, or alertness.

name: Grounding Check-In and Activate
instructions: Use this when you feel spacey or disconnected. 1) Name 5 things you can see, 4 things you can feel, 3 things you can hear, 2 things you can smell, and 1 thing you can taste. 2) Then do 10 small calf raises or heel drops to wake up your lower body. 3) Take three slightly quicker, deeper breaths to bring a bit more energy online. 4) End by touching your horses neck or shoulder and noticing their warmth and smell, reconnecting you to the present moment.

name: Micro-Goal Activation Ride Prep
instructions: When you feel too tired to think about a full ride, shrink the task. 1) Ask yourself: What is the smallest useful thing I could do with my horse today? (for example: 10 minutes of walking with transitions, or 5 minutes of grooming and hand-walking). 2) Say that micro-goal out loud. 3) Take 3 energizing breaths, lifting your chest slightly on the inhale. 4) Start only that micro-goal. 5) If you feel more energy afterward, you may choose to continue—but success is completing the small task you committed to.

name: Gentle Shoulder and Hip Reset
instructions: Use this when your body feels heavy or stiff. 1) Stand with your feet hip-width apart. 2) Roll your shoulders forward and back 5–8 times, slow and easy. 3) Place your hands on your hips and gently circle them 5 times in each direction. 4) Shift your weight from one foot to the other, feeling the ground under each foot. 5) Take 3 slow breaths, letting your exhale be slightly longer than your inhale. 6) Notice if you feel even 10% more awake and willing to move toward your ride.

name: Barn Aisle Stretch and Walk
instructions: For days when you feel drained but still want to show up. 1) Walk down the barn aisle at a relaxed pace. 2) Every 8–10 steps, pause and reach your arms overhead in a comfortable stretch, then let them drop. 3) Gently twist your torso right and left, keeping your hips facing forward. 4) Repeat this walk–stretch–twist cycle for 3–5 minutes. 5) As you move, repeat to yourself: Showing up is enough; small steps count.

name: Mounted Walk Body Wake-Up
instructions: Use this if you feel low energy already in the saddle. 1) At the walk, gently alternately roll each shoulder back, one at a time. 2) Lightly swing your lower leg forward and back within the stirrup to loosen your hips. 3) Do a set of 5–8 light two-point positions at the walk, standing slightly in your stirrups and sitting back down slowly. 4) Take 3 quicker breaths in and out, then settle back into a smoother rhythm. 5) Notice if your body feels more awake and your posture more alive.

name: Why I Ride Values Reminder
instructions: Use this when your motivation feels low. 1) Take a moment with a note app or journal. 2) Write down 3 reasons you ride that have nothing to do with scores or ribbons (for example: connection with my horse, being outdoors, feeling strong in my body). 3) Circle the one that feels most important today. 4) Ask: What is one small action I can take today that honors this value? 5) Commit to that action, even if it is only grooming or a short walk.

name: Values Check When Tired
instructions: When you are exhausted and unsure whether to ride, check in with your values. 1) Rate your physical energy 1–10 and emotional bandwidth 1–10. 2) Ask: Will engaging with my horse in a gentle way today move me closer to the rider and person I want to be? 3) If yes, choose a low-demand activity such as hand-grazing, grooming, or a short walk under saddle. 4) If no, choose a rest action that still honors your value (for example: stretching at home, reading about horsemanship, or planning a future ride).

name: Note from Future Rider Self
instructions: Use this when you doubt whether small efforts matter. 1) Imagine a future version of you 6–12 months from now, riding with more ease and confidence. 2) Ask: What would that future rider thank me for doing today? 3) Write 2–3 short sentences as if they are speaking to you (for example: Thank you for showing up even when you were tired. Those small walks added up.). 4) Choose one tiny step that aligns with that message and do only that today.

name: Training Ride Mindfulness Scan
instructions: Best for training days when your mind is scattered. 1) At the walk, bring your attention to three anchors: your seat in the saddle, your feet in the stirrups, and your hands on the reins. 2) Spend 3–4 breaths focusing on each anchor in turn, noticing sensations without judging them. 3) When your mind wanders to worries or to-do lists, gently bring it back to one anchor. 4) After 2–3 minutes, choose one simple intention for the ride such as: Notice my breath every long side.

name: Arena Edges 5-Senses Grounding
instructions: Use this when you feel mentally far away from your training ride. 1) At the halt or walk, look around the arena and name 4 things you can see (letters, rails, trees). 2) Notice 3 things you can feel (saddle, reins, air on your face). 3) Listen for 2 different sounds (hoof beats, birds, barn noises). 4) Take 1 slow breath and let your shoulders drop. 5) Begin your work from this grounded state, returning to one sense at a time if you drift.

name: Hand-Graze Connection Ritual
instructions: Use this on low-energy or recovery days. 1) Bring your horse to a safe grazing area. 2) While they graze, sync your breathing with their chewing rhythm for 1–2 minutes. 3) Gently stroke their neck or shoulder, paying full attention to the feel of their coat and the movement of their muscles. 4) Spend a few breaths simply appreciating them as your partner, without any agenda. 5) End by thanking them out loud or in your mind for sharing their time and energy with you.

name: In-Hand Focus Circle
instructions: Use this when your horse feels distracted on a training day. 1) In a halter and lead, walk a medium-sized circle together at a calm pace. 2) Each time your horses attention leaves you, gently ask for a small change (for example: halt, step sideways, or change direction) and then return to the circle. 3) Keep your own breathing slow and your shoulders relaxed so you are not adding tension. 4) After 5 minutes, notice whether your horse is checking in with you more frequently.

name: 10-Minute Single Skill Focus
instructions: Ideal for training days with limited energy or time. 1) Choose ONE small skill to work on (for example: walk–halt transitions, straightness on the long side, or rhythm over poles). 2) Set a 10-minute timer. 3) Warm up briefly, then spend the entire 10 minutes experimenting with small adjustments related to that single skill. 4) When the timer ends, cool down and stop—even if it went imperfectly. 5) Mentally note one thing that improved and one thing to try differently next time.

name: Playful Pattern Exploration
instructions: Use this when you want to lighten the mood of training. 1) Set up a very simple pattern: for example, ride a large figure-eight or a serpentine with wide loops. 2) Ride the pattern at the walk, experimenting with different focus points on each pass (for example: one time focus on bend, next on rhythm, next on breathing). 3) Allow some curiosity and playfulness instead of aiming for perfection. 4) After 10–12 minutes, end the ride with a stretchy walk and acknowledge what you and your horse explored together.

name: The 3-Minute Halt (DBT STOP Skill)
instructions:
1. Stop: Pause all action immediately. Do not mount or continue the ride.
2. Take a breath: Inhale slowly through your nose and lengthen the exhale through your mouth.
3. Observe: Notice your thoughts, emotions, body sensations, and your horse's body language.
4. Proceed mindfully: Choose the safest option—full ride, modified ride, groundwork only, or no ride today.
description: A pause-and-reset tool to interrupt emotional escalation and reassess whether it is safe and appropriate to ride, modify, or stop.
evidence_base: DBT distress tolerance (STOP skill), sports psychology crisis reset

name: Temperature Reset (DBT TIP Skill)
instructions:
1. Apply cold water to your wrists, face, or the back of your neck for 20–30 seconds.
2. If possible, step into cool fresh air and focus on slow, steady breathing.
3. Notice changes in your heart rate, muscle tension, and mental intensity.
4. Re-rate your anxiety from 0–10 and decide whether you need additional grounding before riding.
description: A rapid physiological downshift using cold temperature to lower emotional intensity before riding.
evidence_base: DBT TIP skills, autonomic nervous system regulation research

name: Groundwork First Rule
instructions:
1. Lead your horse at the walk for 3–5 minutes, focusing on a calm rhythm and clear boundaries.
2. Add simple yielding or backing exercises to check connection and responsiveness.
3. Notice your own breathing, tension, and thoughts as you move with your horse.
4. Observe your horse's signals—head position, muscle tone, responsiveness, and startle level.
5. Decide whether today is appropriate for a full ride, a modified ride, or groundwork only.
description: A co-regulation routine using simple groundwork to assess emotional safety and readiness for riding.
evidence_base: Somatic regulation, groundwork-based horsemanship, equine-assisted therapy principles

name: Name It to Tame It
instructions:
1. Pause and complete the sentence: "I am feeling ____ because ____." Say it silently or out loud.
2. Acknowledge that the emotion is valid without judging it as good or bad.
3. Remind yourself: "This emotion does not get to control my choices with my horse."
4. Take three slow breaths and check whether your emotional intensity has shifted.
description: A cognitive-emotional tool where the rider labels their emotions to reduce overwhelm and regain clarity.
evidence_base: Affect labeling research, neuropsychology of emotion regulation

name: 5-4-3-2-1 Sensory Anchors (Rider Edition)
instructions:
1. Name 5 things you can see around you (e.g., arena rails, mountains, saddle, your horse's ears).
2. Identify 4 things you can hear (hoofbeats, wind, voices, barn sounds).
3. Notice 3 things you can touch (reins, your boots, your horse's coat or mane).
4. Identify 2 scents you can smell (hay, leather, fresh air).
5. Choose 1 grounding movement (press your heels into the ground, roll your shoulders, or place a hand on your horse's neck) and take a slow exhale.
description: A grounding exercise using the barn and arena environment to bring attention back to the present moment.
evidence_base: Grounding techniques, trauma-informed stabilization, mindfulness-based stress reduction

name: Wise Mind Saddle Check
instructions:
1. Emotion Mind: Ask yourself, "What do I feel like doing right now with my horse?" Notice impulses such as pushing through or avoiding.
2. Reasonable Mind: Ask, "Given my current state and my horse's behavior, what is the safest and most realistic plan?"
3. Wise Mind: Blend both and ask, "What choice honors both safety and partnership?"
4. Clearly state your decision (e.g., full ride, walk-only ride, groundwork, or no ride) and commit to it for this session.
description: A DBT-based decision tool to integrate emotion and logic before making a riding plan.
evidence_base: DBT Wise Mind model, decision-making under stress in sport

name: ACT Open the Door Exercise
instructions:
1. Visualize a door in front of you labeled with your current emotion (e.g., anxiety, anger, grief).
2. Imagine gently opening the door and allowing the emotion to be present without fighting or suppressing it.
3. Ask yourself, "What value do I want to ride from today?" (e.g., safety, patience, connection, kindness, learning).
4. Choose one small, concrete action that reflects that value—for example, a quiet walk ride, focused grooming, or simple groundwork.
description: An acceptance-based practice that allows difficult emotions while choosing values-guided action with the horse.
evidence_base: Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT), values-based behavior change

name: Sports Psychology Performance Reset
instructions:
1. Notice unhelpful thoughts, such as "I'm a bad rider" or "This ride will go badly."
2. Internally say "Stop" or imagine a stop sign to interrupt the spiral.
3. Choose a simple cue word or phrase like "steady," "soft," "breathe," or "present."
4. Take one slow breath and repeat your cue word on the exhale as you return to the next small task with your horse.
description: A quick cue-based reset to interrupt negative self-talk and restore present-moment focus.
evidence_base: Sports psychology self-talk interventions, performance routines research

name: Co-Regulation Through Body Position
instructions:
1. Stand or sit with your feet grounded and briefly scan for tension in your jaw, shoulders, chest, back, and legs.
2. Soften your jaw, drop your shoulders, and allow your chest and ribcage to gently expand.
3. Take several slow exhales, imagining the breath traveling down into your seat and legs.
4. While near or on your horse, maintain this softened posture and notice any changes in your horse's breathing, expression, or muscle tone.
description: A somatic tool that uses posture and breath to send safety cues to the horse's nervous system.
evidence_base: Polyvagal theory, somatic regulation, equine-assisted psychotherapy observations

name: Ride Alternatives Menu
instructions:
1. Create a personal list of alternatives such as: grooming only, hand-walking, in-hand trail, groundwork, walk-only ride, or no ride today.
2. Before mounting, rate your emotional intensity from 0–10.
3. If your number is above your chosen safety threshold (for example, 6 or higher), commit to selecting one alternative instead of a full schooling ride.
4. After the session, briefly reflect on how your emotional state and your horse's behavior changed using the alternative plan.
description: A structured safety plan offering pre-chosen alternatives when emotional intensity is too high for a full ride.
evidence_base: Risk management in sport, DBT crisis planning, equine welfare guidelines

name: 5-Minute Nervous System Reset
description: A structured 5-minute sequence that helps riders assess and regulate their nervous system before deciding whether to ride, modify, or choose groundwork.
instructions:
Minute 1 — BREATH:
Inhale for a count of 4 and exhale for a count of 6. Repeat slowly.

Minute 2 — BODY:
Drop your shoulders, soften your jaw, and loosen the grip of your hands.

Minute 3 — SENSORY RESET:
Name 3 things you see, 2 things you hear, and 1 thing you can touch.

Minute 4 — CONNECTION:
Place a hand on your horse's shoulder or neck and match your breathing to a calm rhythm.

Minute 5 — DECISION:
Ask yourself: "Do I feel safe? Does my horse feel safe? What is the kindest choice for both of us?" Then choose: Ride, Groundwork, or No ride.
evidence_base: Breath-based regulation, grounding techniques, co-regulation with horses, applied sports psychology routines

name: Pre-Ride Emotional Check-In
description: A brief self-assessment to help riders identify emotional state, triggers, body sensations, horse feedback, and choose the safest, kindest ride plan.
instructions:
1. What am I feeling emotionally right now?
Write your answer.

2. On a scale of 1–10, what is my emotional intensity?
Circle or note a number from 1–10.

3. What triggered or contributed to my current state?
Describe any events, thoughts, or stressors.

4. What physical sensations do I notice in my body?
Write the sensations (e.g., tight chest, shaky hands, tense jaw).

5. What is my horse showing me right now?
Describe your horse's behavior, expression, and energy.

6. What is one thing I need before deciding to ride? (e.g., breathing, grounding, pause, drinking water, going outside.)
Write your answer.

7. If I ride, what is the safest, kindest plan for me and my horse?
Describe the plan (e.g., walk-only ride, light schooling, groundwork, or no ride).
evidence_base: Self-monitoring and emotional awareness assessments, CBT/DBT-informed check-ins, sports psychology pre-performance routines

name: Is This a Riding Day? Self-Assessment
instructions: Use this checklist to assess whether today is a safe day to ride. Check each item that describes you today. MENTAL STATE: My thoughts are racing. I feel overwhelmed or emotionally flooded. I am catastrophizing or thinking in extremes. I feel disconnected, numb, or checked out. EMOTIONAL SIGNS: I feel anxious, irritable, or on edge. I feel dread approaching the barn. I feel pressure to push through. BODY SIGNS: I feel shaky, hot, tight, or lightheaded. My breathing is shallow or fast. I feel physically tense. HORSE FEEDBACK: My horse seems tense, watchy, or reactive. My horse is not standing still or is hyper-alert. My horse is mirroring my tension. DECISION GUIDE: If 3 or more items are checked, use distress tolerance tools (like STOP, Temperature Reset, or Groundwork First) before deciding to ride. If 5 or more items are checked, choose groundwork or no ride today for safety. This is not weakness. This is wisdom.

name: Emergency Ground-Tie & Breathe
description: A mounted crisis tool for when the rider feels near panic or emotional overload and needs to rapidly stabilize and keep both horse and rider safe.
instructions:
1. If it is safe to do so, bring your horse to a halt in the safest available spot (center of arena, away from traffic or obstacles).
2. Shorten your reins just enough to maintain control without pulling, and sit deep in the saddle.
3. Take 3–5 slow breaths: inhale through your nose for a count of 4, exhale through your mouth for a count of 6.
4. Silently repeat a grounding phrase such as: "I am here, I am on my horse, we are standing, we are safe right now."
5. Scan for danger: if any real safety risk is present (loose horses, severe spook, unstable footing), dismount calmly and move both of you to a safer area.
6. Once stable, decide whether to continue at the walk only, switch to groundwork, or end the ride for today.
evidence_base: DBT crisis survival skills, grounding, breath-based autonomic regulation, equestrian risk management practices

name: Barn Safe Space Time-Out
description: A short, structured time-out away from the horse to prevent escalation when the rider feels on the verge of losing emotional control.
instructions:
1. Ensure your horse is secured safely (cross-ties, stall, or safe tie location) before stepping away.
2. Tell yourself clearly: "I am taking a 5-minute time-out to keep both of us safe." This frames the pause as a skill, not a failure.
3. Move to a pre-chosen safe space at the barn (tack room, bathroom, car, quiet corner) where you can be physically away from stimuli.
4. Use a grounding sequence while away: identify 3 things you see, 2 things you hear, and 1 thing you feel physically (chair, wall, floor under feet).
5. Take at least 5 slow breaths, lengthening the exhale.
6. At the end of the time-out, ask yourself: "Am I calm enough to return and choose a safe plan—groundwork, gentle ride, or no ride today?"
evidence_base: DBT crisis time-out strategies, anger management, environmental modification for emotional regulation

name: Crisis Ride Stop Plan (Dismount & Decompress)
description: A clear plan for safely ending a ride in progress when emotions or fear become too intense to continue mounted work.
instructions:
1. Acknowledge the crisis without judgment: silently say, "This is too much for me right now. Stopping is a smart, safe choice."
2. Bring your horse to a walk and then a controlled halt in the safest available location.
3. Dismount calmly and deliberately, keeping your breathing slow throughout the movement.
4. Lead your horse at the walk for 2–3 minutes, allowing both of your nervous systems to downshift while you stay in motion.
5. Once both of you are calmer, move to a safe area (grooming area, stall, or quiet corner) and untack or loosen tack as appropriate.
6. Briefly debrief with yourself: what signs did you notice in your body and thoughts that told you it was time to stop? What did your horse show you? Log this as a success in using a safety plan, not a failure.
evidence_base: DBT crisis planning, graded exposure with safety stops, equestrian safety and fall-prevention guidelines

name: Call-and-Connect Support Script
description: A phone-based connection script to prevent isolation and help the rider co-regulate with a trusted person during or after a barn crisis.
instructions:
1. Identify 1–3 safe people ahead of time (coach, barn friend, therapist, partner) who are willing to be in your support list.
2. When your distress feels too big to manage alone (e.g., shaking, crying, overwhelmed), step away to a safe spot and call or text one person on your list.
3. Use this simple script: "Hey, I'm at the barn and I'm really overwhelmed right now. My distress is about a ___ out of 10. I don't need you to fix it—I just need you to listen for a few minutes while I calm down."
4. While on the call, focus on slowing your breathing and describing concrete facts (what happened, what your horse did, what you did) instead of global self-criticism.
5. End the call by naming one next step: "I'm going to do groundwork only," or "I'm going to groom and then go home," or "I'm going to sit in my car and listen to music for 10 minutes."
6. Thank your support person and note that reaching out was a skillful crisis tool, not a burden.
evidence_base: Social support buffering research, DBT phone coaching principles, co-regulation science

name: Flashback Anchor Kit
description: A sensory and cognitive grounding protocol for riders who experience trauma-related flashbacks, vivid memories, or intense fear spikes at the barn.
instructions:
